title: Data-centre builders borrowed more as chipmakers repaid debt during the AI investment boom
bank: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis
summary: Did the firms building artificial intelligence infrastructure borrow to pay for it, or did they spend cash that was already on their balance sheets? Julian Kozlowski, Masataka Mori, Juan M. Sánchez and Nicholas Sullivan show why neither description fits the whole industry. Using financial statements for publicly traded US companies, they trace where investment increased, which firms generated the additional cash and how they changed their borrowing and payouts. Operating cash generation rose enough to cover the increase in investment across the ten large technology firms the paper calls hyperscalers. The six data-centre builders faced a quite different financing problem from the three semiconductor producers.

Table 1 describes up to 140,414 annual observations on 13,731 firms and up to 267,369 quarterly observations on 8,338 firms. The authors exclude finance, real estate, utilities and public administration. They measure cash and short-term investments relative to assets. Their broad investment measure includes capital spending, research and development, and acquisitions. It therefore captures more than spending on data centres. The fall in cash was concentrated among formerly cash-rich firms. The 90th percentile of the asset-weighted cash ratio fell from around 40% in 2016–19 to 24% in 2025, while the median changed little. The investment ratio for firms in the largest 1% by sales rose from around 13% to 22% over the same comparison.

Table 2 compares cash and subsequent investment across technological eras. A ten-percentage-point higher cash-to-assets ratio was associated with 3.2 percentage points more investment relative to assets the following year in the AI period, against about 2.2 points in the PC and internet eras. R&D accounts for most of the stronger relationship. This comparison does not establish that managers accumulated cash in anticipation of AI or that running down cash caused the investment surge. Figure 10 shows that hyperscalers’ cash ratios were already declining before ChatGPT’s release, falling from about 35% in 2018 to 16% in early 2026. Figure 11 separates the investment boom into an earlier phase led by research spending and a later acceleration led by capital expenditure.

The financing account in Table 4 compares average quarterly flows in GDP-deflated dollars over 2012 Q1–2018 Q4 and 2024 Q4–2026 Q2. Across the ten firms, investment rose from $52.99 billion to $227.83 billion per quarter. The table’s measure of internally generated resources, operating cash flow plus R&D, rose from $73.69 billion to $274.83 billion. Adding R&D back to cash flow matters because the authors also include it on the investment side. Apple is in the ten-firm total but in neither of the two subgroups. The subgroup results therefore need not sum to the aggregate.

The builders’ quarterly investment increased by $161.79 billion, while their adjusted operating flow rose by $153.06 billion. Their net debt issuance increased from $3.23 billion to $30.17 billion per quarter. Shareholder payouts actually rose in dollars, but fell from 27.1% to 13.6% of operating resources. Semiconductor producers’ corresponding cash-flow increase comfortably exceeded the increase in investment, and their net debt issuance went from positive $1.10 billion to negative $0.79 billion per quarter. Figure 13 reinforces the split using free cash flow, defined there as operating cash flow less capital expenditure relative to assets. The paper’s recorded flows omit commitments including future leases and purchase obligations. Assessing individual builders’ financing needs requires those future claims as well as the cash spent so far.

questions.question: How much investment is still to be funded after signed commitments are included?
questions.detail: Reconcile each builder’s reported capital spending with lease commitments, equipment purchase obligations, construction schedules and remaining contractual payments in company filings. Separate commitments already included in creditors or lease liabilities from genuinely additional obligations. A firm with strong current operating cash flow can still face a financing gap if cash payments fall due before new capacity earns revenue.

questions.question: Does the difference between builders and chipmakers survive a comparison at the same point in their investment cycles?
questions.detail: Extend Figure 13 with consistent, firm-level quarterly measures of cash from operations, capital expenditure and working capital. Compare the timing of supplier sales with the timing of customer payment and data-centre utilisation. A temporary timing difference would predict the groups’ free-cash-flow ratios converging after capacity is installed, while persistent divergence would support a more structural difference in financing needs.

questions.question: What determines which firms use debt rather than further reducing payouts or cash accumulation?
questions.detail: Compare firm-level debt issuance, maturities, cash balances, net repurchases and recurring commitments around investment announcements, keeping Table 4’s R&D adjustment consistent. Separate a change in the level of payouts from a change in their share of cash flow. Higher issuance alongside larger dollar payouts can reflect a choice about shareholder distributions as well as a shortage of internal funds.
